summary: Hostile audit #13 — SERVICES, dual mode: defects AND the implementation contract
logs: 59 candidates from 6/6 finders; 56 clean areas; 6 contract blocks

survived.title: get_manager() is re-fetched after a device-length await, so a config-entry reload mid-dispatch loses the just-started job record (or raises a bare KeyError)
survived.mechanism: `_common.get_manager(hass)` is a bare subscript: `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]` (_common.py:35). Five job_control handlers call it TWICE with a real await in between — e.g. `_handle_start_selected_rooms`: line 152 `payload = await get_manager(hass).start_selected_rooms(...)`, then line 156 `await get_manager(hass).async_save()`. This is a gap ACROSS an await, not a synchronous claim. The awaited call is long: core/manager.py:4921 `start_selected_rooms` awaits `_run_global_pre_calls`, `_resolve_live_dispatch_payload`, `_dispatch_clean_payload` and an executor job — it physically commands the robot — and it writes the new job into `self.data['active_jobs'][vac][map_id]` IN MEMORY ONLY (verified: no async_save inside; the handler's line 156 is the only persist). If the config entry reloads during that window (`__init__.py:462` `_async_update_listener` on any options change; the Reload button; or `services/setup.py:165` `setup_add_vacuum`, which explicitly does `hass.async_create_task(hass.config_entries.async_reload(...))`), then either (a) DATA_RUNTIME has been popped (__init__.py:542; `hass.data[DOMAIN]` itself is popped at :546) and line 156 raises an unhandled KeyError, or (b) setup has already re-run and line 156 returns the NEW manager, whose `async_save()` writes storage-loaded data — silently overwriting the storage without the active-job record. Same shape at lines 162/166, 189/193, 200/204, 212/234. `hass.services.async_remove` does not cancel or await in-flight handlers, so the handler outlives the unload.
survived.user_impact: The robot is cleaning but the integration has no active-job record: the card shows no run in progress, no per-room progress or attribution, no learning sample, and no finalization. In path (b) nothing is logged at all — a clean success response with the job silently gone. In path (a) the user gets a raw `KeyError` traceback in the log because line 156 sits OUTSIDE the handler's try/except (lines 151-154).
survived.guards_checked: `_handle_start_selected_rooms`'s try/except (job_control.py:151-154) wraps ONLY the start call — the save at 156 is outside it, so neither path is converted to a HomeAssistantError. `_common.get_manager` (line 35-37) has no `.get()` fallback and no None handling, unlike the sibling pattern in services/setup.py and services/errors.py which use `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_RUNTIME)` and return a graceful shape. `async_unload_entry` (__init__.py:492 then :542) removes services BEFORE popping DATA_RUNTIME, which is correct ordering for NEW calls but does nothing for an already-running handler. `entry.runtime_data = manager` exists (__init__.py:317) as the idiomatic per-entry handle but no handler uses it. core/manager.py:4921 read in full to confirm start_selected_rooms never persists itself.
survived.area: WIRE — registration, teardown and the shared spine (services/__init__.py, services/_common.py, services/debug.py, registration survey across all 13 domain modules)

survived.title: resolved_call_data's docstring claims an unresolvable map_id always raises; discover_rooms is the one consumer that silently falls through and persists the payload under an empty-string map key
survived.mechanism: `resolved_call_data` (_common.py:40-76) documents: "active_map entity missing or sentinel-valued -> returned unchanged; the manager method will raise its own clear error on the missing kwarg, which is the desired behavior (silent fallback to a wrong map would be worse)." That is a CLAIM about 46 downstream manager entry points. I enumerated every method reached via `**resolved_call_data(...)` and checked each signature: all declare `map_id` as a required keyword-only arg (so a missing map_id does raise TypeError, caught and surfaced) EXCEPT two — `dispatch_zone_clean` (core/manager.py:4828, `map_id: str | None = None`, deliberate and documented at job_control.py:120) and `discover_rooms` (rooms/room_crud.py:41, `map_id: str | None = None`), which is NOT deliberate. When the adapter's `active_map` entity exists in the state machine but reads `unknown`/`unavailable`, `get_active_map_id` returns None early (rooms/room_discovery.py:69-74 via `is_blank_state`, entity_helpers.py:39-41 — the blank set includes "unknown" and "unavailable") and never reaches the `_implicit_attribute_map_id` fallback. `resolved_call_data` then returns the data with no map_id key. `room_crud.discover_rooms` proceeds anyway: `discover_rooms_payload` returns `active_map_id: None` (room_discovery.py:268-283), and line 61 computes `_disc_map_id = str(payload.get('active_map_id') or map_id or '')` = `""`, then line 74 writes `data['discovery'][vac][''] = payload`. The service handler (services/rooms.py:154) then `await manager.async_save()`s that junk bucket to durable storage.
survived.user_impact: Pressing "Discover rooms" — exactly what a user does when the active_map sensor is stale/unavailable — returns a clean success (the service is registered without supports_response, and the handler's `except Exception -> HomeAssistantError` at rooms.py:141 never fires because nothing raises). The rooms are cached under `""` while every reader (room_crud.py:132/233/365/412, setup/drift.py) keys by the real map id, so the setup panel shows zero discovered rooms with no error, and a stale `discovery[""]` bucket is persisted permanently.
survived.guards_checked: `_DISCOVER_ROOMS_SCHEMA` (services/rooms.py:64-69) declares `map_id` Optional, so voluptuous does not reject the omission. `resolved_call_data`'s early return at _common.py:74-76 returns data unchanged rather than raising. `_handle_discover_rooms`'s try/except (rooms.py:139-142) only catches exceptions — there are none on this path. The `run_discovery_pass` call is separately wrapped in a best-effort except (rooms.py:147-152). `get_active_map_id`'s registry fallback (room_discovery.py:79-90) is only reached when the entity is ABSENT from the state machine, not when it is present-but-blank. None rescue it.

survived.title: Sixteen registered services documented as public API have no services.yaml descriptor, including set_dock_event_count whose five dock siblings all have one
survived.mechanism: There is exactly one services.yaml (verified by find). An AST sweep of every `hass.services.async_register(DOMAIN, ...)` call site versus the services.yaml keys shows 16 registered names with no entry: all ten `setup_*` (services/setup.py:353-392), `save_adapter_config`, `delete_adapter_config`, `get_adapter_config`, `discover_adapter_entities`, `observe_entity_states` (services/adapter_config.py:229-262), and `set_dock_event_count` (services/dock.py:174). All 16 ARE documented as callable in docs/advanced/03-services.md. This is not a policy of hiding internal services: `get_vacuum_capabilities`, registered in the same adapter_config block, DOES have a services.yaml entry, and the five dock siblings of `set_dock_event_count` (wash_mop, dry_mop, empty_dust, stop_dry_mop, get_dock_action_status) all do too — so the one dock service that MUTATES a stored counter is the only one without a descriptor.
survived.user_impact: A YAML author who follows docs/advanced/03-services.md to `set_dock_event_count` or any setup_* service finds it in Developer Tools -> Actions with no name, no description, and no field UI — just a bare data editor with no hint of the allowed `event_type` values (which the voluptuous schema restricts to three literals). No runtime failure, but the documented surface and the HA-side surface disagree.
survived.guards_checked: Confirmed only one services.yaml exists; confirmed the docs file names all 16; confirmed get_vacuum_capabilities and the five dock siblings are present in services.yaml, ruling out an intentional 'internal services are undescribed' convention. Voluptuous schemas do exist for all 16, so the calls themselves are still validated — the gap is purely the descriptor.

survived.title: get_room_profiles is the only one of the 79 registrations with no schema, so caller-supplied scoping arguments are accepted and silently ignored
survived.mechanism: `hass.services.async_register(DOMAIN, SERVICE_GET_ROOM_PROFILES, get_room_profiles, supports_response=True)` passes no `schema=`. An AST sweep across all 13 domain modules confirms this is the sole registration in the package without one (every other of the 79 has a voluptuous schema; even the two no-argument debug services use an explicit `vol.Schema({})`). With schema=None HA performs no validation, so any `call.data` is accepted; the handler `_handle_get_room_profiles` (line 115) then calls `get_manager(hass).get_room_profiles()` with no arguments and discards the data entirely.
survived.user_impact: A caller who passes `vacuum_entity_id` or `map_id` — a reasonable assumption given that every neighbouring room-profile service requires `vacuum_entity_id` — gets the global profile library back with no indication the argument was ignored. Compare `setup_get_status`, which is also argument-free but declares `vol.Schema({})` (services/setup.py:86) and therefore REJECTS extra keys.

survived.title: The debug-capture auto-stop timer is not cancelled on unload, so an orphaned timer from before a reload kills a capture started after it
survived.mechanism: `register_debug_services` builds a closure-local `autostop = {'cancel': None}` (line 483) and stores an `async_call_later` handle in it (line 510) when the caller passes `max_minutes`. `services/debug.py:31` calls `register_debug_services` on every `register(hass)`, i.e. on every config-entry setup — so a reload creates a FRESH `autostop` dict, and `_cancel_autostop` (line 485) can only ever see the new one. Nothing cancels the pending timer: it is not registered via `entry.async_on_unload`, and `async_unload_entry` (__init__.py:496-499) calls `get_capture().stop()` but never touches the timer. `DebugCapture` is a process-wide singleton (`get_capture`, line 404), so when the orphaned timer fires it calls `stop()` on whatever capture is live at that moment.
survived.user_impact: User starts a capture with `max_minutes: 60`, reloads the integration, starts a new capture — the new capture silently stops at the old timer's deadline, logged only as 'debug capture auto-stopped after 60 min'. Diagnostic tooling only; no user data affected.
survived.guards_checked: `_cancel_autostop` (debug_capture.py:485-488) reads only the current closure's dict. `services/debug.py` has no `remove()`/teardown entry point at all — `services/__init__.py:66-71` only calls `hass.services.async_remove` per name, so a module cannot run any other cleanup on unload. `DebugCapture.stop()` (line 249-271) is idempotent, so the double-stop itself is safe; the loss is the ACTIVE capture, not corruption.

survived.title: start_selected_rooms discards every refusal — no supports_response, no exception, DEBUG log only; docs promise a response it cannot return
survived.mechanism: `_handle_start_selected_rooms` (line 149) awaits `manager.start_selected_rooms(...)` into a local `payload`, logs it at DEBUG (line 155), and returns `None`. The registration at lines 321-324 is the ONLY one of the three start services with no `supports_response=True` (start_run_profile line 327 and start_zone_clean line 331 both have it). manager.start_selected_rooms never raises on a refusal — it RETURNS `{"started": False, "reason": ...}` for every soft-refuse path: `blocked` (core/manager.py:4943 — active_job_running, vacuum_busy, mid_job_service, map_mismatch, no_rooms_selected, invalid_payload, onboarding_required, job_paused, all_selected_rooms_blocked, incomplete_access_graph, access_graph_required), `confirmation_required` (4960), and `vacuum_missing` (4989). All of those dicts are dropped on the floor. The service then still calls `async_save()` and returns success to HA. docs/advanced/03-services.md:29 states "the service returns `confirmation_required: true` with a `confirm_token`" and line 24 documents `confirm_token` as "Retry token returned by a prior `confirmation_required` response" — that response is unreachable; HA rejects `response_variable` on a non-response-capable service, which the card's own comment at src/actions/rooms.js:55 confirms.
survived.user_impact: An automation that calls `eufy_vacuum.start_selected_rooms` at 09:00 gets a green checkmark whether the robot started or was refused for any of eleven reasons. The house is not cleaned, no error, no notification, nothing in the log above DEBUG. The documented recovery workflow (read confirmation_required, retry with confirm_token) is impossible on this service — the token can only be obtained by separately calling get_start_status first, which the docs never say.
survived.guards_checked: Registration lines 317-364 (only start_selected_rooms and clear_active_job among the twelve lack supports_response); handler lines 149-156 (try/except only converts a RAISE, and the refusal paths do not raise); core/manager.py start_selected_rooms 4938-5149 (returns dicts, raises nothing on refusal); jobs/job_monitor.py build_start_blocker_from_lifecycle 233-308 (confirms a running job blocks via `active_job_running`, i.e. the block is correct — only its reporting is lost); src/actions/rooms.js startCleaning 60-108 (card compensates by calling get_start_status first and checking `.blocked`, then fires start_selected_rooms blind — so even the card cannot see a state change between the two calls); services.yaml start_selected_rooms block (no response declaration).

survived.title: start_zone_clean is the only start service with zero preconditions — it dispatches to the robot mid-job and strands the tracked room job
survived.mechanism: `_handle_start_zone_clean` calls `manager.dispatch_zone_clean(**resolved_call_data(...))` directly. Its two siblings both route through `get_start_status` first (start_selected_rooms via manager.start_selected_rooms:4938; start_run_profile via the same call). start_zone_clean routes through neither, and `dispatch/manager.py dispatch_zone_clean` (86-245) validates ONLY geometry and adapter capability — rect shape, degenerate-area, zone_command presence, zone_max count, coordinate inversion, per-zone side/area bounds. There is no read of the active job, the lifecycle state, or the vacuum state anywhere on the path. The module docstring at job_control.py:7 calls it "fire-and-forget, no job tracking" and the manager docstring at 4822 says it "deliberately BYPASSES the job/queue/learning pipeline" — that framing covers what it does NOT write, but nothing covers what it OVERRIDES.
survived.user_impact: Called while a tracked room job is running, the robot abandons the in-flight room clean and starts a zone clean, while the integration's active_job stays `started` with its full room list, timers, and counter/pose sample buffers. When the device docks, the lifecycle listener finalizes the ROOM job against the zone run's durations and battery delta — the learning record is written for rooms that were never cleaned, and the completed rooms are attributed wrongly. No warning is shown at any point; the service returns `{"status": "dispatched"}` which looks like a clean success.

survived.title: clear_active_job destroys a running job's record unconditionally and returns nothing — no status precondition, no supports_response, immediate persist
survived.mechanism: `_handle_clear_active_job` calls `manager.clear_active_job(**resolved_call_data(...))`, discards the returned dict into a DEBUG log, then `await get_manager(hass).async_save()` — persisting the deletion to storage. Registration at line 345-348 uses VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA with no supports_response. `jobs/active_job.py clear_active_job` (1862-1883) has NO status guard: it unconditionally overwrites `data["active_jobs"][vac][map]` with `_default_active_job_state(...)`, discarding started_at, battery_start, job_id, resolved_rooms, completed_room_ids, phases, counter samples and pose samples — whether the job is `started`, `paused`, or already empty. Its sibling `cancel_active_job` finalizes and archives before clearing; this one only discards. The docs (03-services.md:667) scope it to "a stuck or orphaned job state ... when the vacuum has already finished", but nothing in the code enforces that scope, and the same doc paragraph contradicts itself — line 660 says "Persists to storage" while line 667 says "it only removes the in-memory record".
survived.user_impact: A user or automation clearing what they believe is a stale job while the robot is actually mid-run permanently loses that run's learning data — the run is never finalized, per-room durations are gone, and the incomplete-run log is never written, so retry_missed_rooms has nothing to act on. The robot keeps cleaning with no integration-side record. Because there is no response, the caller cannot even tell whether there WAS a live job it just destroyed.

In start_selected_rooms the writes to `data["queue"]`, `data["payloads"]` and `data["active_jobs"]` land at core/manager.py 4979-4984 and 5060-5062, and `_dispatch_clean_payload` (5021) has already sent the clean command to the robot, before code that can still raise: `get_planned_job_estimate` (5054), `apply_per_room_live_settings` (5102), `_clear_room_selections_after_start` (5112). survived.user_impact: The robot is cleaning, the user sees a red "Failed to start cleaning: …" error, and the active job exists only in RAM. The error message also misrepresents what happened — the start did not fail, a post-dispatch step did.

`_handle_observe_entity_states` (adapter_config.py:166) returns a distinguishable shape for a missing entity (`state: None` vs a real state string, which HA never renders as None) and does not raise on an unknown id. `discover_adapter_entities` behaves exactly as docs/advanced/03-services.md:1561 describes it, including the substring-match semantics.

`get_setup_status` degrades cleanly when the manager is absent, returning a well-formed empty state (`setup_complete: False`, `state: 'no_vacuums'`, `next_actions: ['add_vacuum']`) rather than raising — status.py:161-169. It is a pure in-memory read with no I/O, so it is safe on the event loop.

`_common.resolved_call_data`'s three documented pass-through cases are each individually correct (map_id present → unchanged; vacuum_entity_id missing → unchanged; unresolvable active map → unchanged). The only defect is the docstring's claim about who raises afterwards (SETUP-7); the resolver logic itself is sound.

`config_loader.load_stored_adapter_configs` (:26-64) is defensively written: it type-checks each stored config, logs and skips malformed entries, and wraps each registration in try/except so one bad row cannot take the integration down at startup.

Registration/teardown symmetry: both modules' `SERVICES` tuples exactly match what `register()` registers (run_profiles 7/7, snapshots 4/4), so `services/__init__.async_unregister_services` removes everything on unload — no orphaned service after a reload.

supports_response coverage: all 11 registrations in these two modules declare `supports_response=True` and every handler returns a dict, so no caller can hit HA's 'service does not support response' error, and no handler returns None.

services.yaml completeness for this area: all 7 run-profile services and all 4 snapshot services have a services.yaml entry with matching field names and required flags — nothing here is registered-but-invisible in Developer Tools.

async_save discipline on mutating calls: every mutating handler in both modules (save/apply/rename/overwrite/delete/set_steps, set_pause_timeout_settings) awaits `get_manager(hass).async_save()` after the manager call, and the pure-read handlers do not — the persistence side of the pattern is applied consistently (the defects above are about WHAT gets persisted, not whether).

Event-loop safety of get_dashboard_snapshot: the handler correctly pre-warms the blocking .storage read via `await manager.async_refresh_map_state_source(...)` and then calls the sync snapshot on-loop; the comment explaining why `async_add_executor_job` must NOT be used (get_dashboard_snapshot fires bus events internally) matches the code, and `async_refresh_map_state_source`'s 'never raises' claim is backed by a real try/except around the backend dispatch (mapping/map_source_coordinator.py:181).

pause-timeout value handling: `_PAUSE_TIMEOUT_SETTINGS_SCHEMA`'s `vol.All(vol.Coerce(int), vol.Range(min=0))` matches `_normalize_pause_timeout_minutes` (max(int,0)) and the consumer's `if pause_timeout_minutes <= 0: return` disabled-semantics (jobs/active_job.py:2303); it is also consistent with the sibling `pause_timeout_minutes_override` schemas in job_control.py:86,106. No upper bound, but a large value only means 'never times out'.

apply_run_profile's profile_not_found path, and the same path in rename/overwrite/delete, correctly raise `ServiceValidationError` (the user-facing HA error class) rather than HomeAssistantError or a silent return — the four are consistent with each other and covered by tests SRN-5/7/8/10.

No cross-await state assumption in either module: each handler resolves call data, makes one manager call, saves, returns. The only await-gap (snapshots.py:62 -> 66) reads a cache the awaited call itself populated; nothing here holds a lock or a pre-await snapshot of mutable job state across the gap.

Dock action gating vocabulary is genuinely adapter-driven, not brand-hardcoded: `_vocab_set` (dock/manager.py:160-164) reads `dock_events.triggers` per key and returns an EMPTY frozenset when the adapter omits it, with an explicit comment that an omitting adapter gets no detection rather than inheriting Eufy's vocabulary. Verified against both adapters — Roborock omits the block and correctly gets empty sets rather than Eufy states.

`_check_dock_action` (services/dock.py:64-74) correctly converts a blocked gated action into `ServiceValidationError` carrying the manager's own `message`, so a genuinely-blocked wash/dry/empty is surfaced to the user as a validation error rather than a success-shaped response. Its `payload.get("allowed", True)` default is safe: every `_async_run_dock_action` return path sets `allowed` explicitly.

`reset_maintenance` preserves a user-set `interval_hours` across a reset (maintenance/manager.py:673-680) rather than replacing the component entry wholesale, and the comment documenting why matches the code exactly. I checked every other writer to `data["maintenance"][vacuum][component]` (number.py:232-239, services/maintenance.py:92-94, maintenance/manager.py:624) — `interval_hours` is the only key any of them writes, so the rebuild loses nothing else.

`reset_maintenance` has real three-way validation with distinct honest reasons: `no_source_entity` (escalated by the handler to ServiceValidationError), `source_unavailable`, and `invalid_usage_hours` (maintenance/manager.py:640-667), each with `reset: False` and a `reason` the caller can branch on. This is the strongest validation surface in the three modules.

`ErrorTracker.acknowledge` guards `if vacuum_entity_id not in root: return False` before `_ensure_record`, so unlike get_recent_errors it does not fabricate storage records for unknown entity ids. The mid-run MARK-don't-delete behaviour itself is correct and thoroughly justified in-code; the defect is only that the service's response and docstrings never caught up (DIAG-4).

`_persist_and_notify` (core/error_tracker.py:1059-1074) correctly schedules the save via `hass.loop.call_soon_threadsafe(hass.async_create_task, ...)` so `acknowledge_error` persists from the loop thread without the service handler needing its own `async_save` — the asymmetry with dock/maintenance (which do call async_save explicitly) is deliberate and works.

`get_active_run_latch` / `get_last_device_latch` return `copy.deepcopy` of the latch, so nothing the error services or their downstream presentation surfaces hold can be mutated by a later tracker write. Verified the deep (not shallow) copy — the nesting is where the aliasing lived.

DockManager's `self._data = manager.data` alias (dock/manager.py:57) is safe: `self.data` is assigned exactly once in EufyVacuumManager (core/manager.py:313, inside async_initialize) and DockManager is constructed at line 357, after it. No reload path reassigns `manager.data`, so the alias cannot go stale and dock counter writes always land in the object that gets saved.

All ten registrations across the three modules declare `supports_response=True` and every handler returns a dict on its success path, so no caller of these services hits HA's "service does not support responses" error. Registration follows the package contract uniformly: module-level `SERVICES` tuple + `register(hass)` closure wrapper per service.

`resolved_call_data`'s pass-through policy is correct in principle — it refuses to invent a map_id when the active-map entity is sentinel-valued or registered-but-stateless, explicitly preferring failure over silently acting on the wrong map. The defect (DIAG-7) is purely in how that refusal is surfaced, not in the decision.

contract.area: WIRE — registration, teardown and the shared spine (services/__init__.py, services/_common.py, services/debug.py, registration survey across all 13 domain modules)

notes.pattern: A service module is a flat file in `custom_components/eufy_vacuum/services/` exposing exactly two public names: `SERVICES: tuple[str, ...]` and `register(hass: HomeAssistant) -> None`. Service NAMES are constants in `const.py` (`SERVICE_<UPPER>` = "<lower>"), never string literals in the module. `services/__init__.py` imports the module, lists it in the `_DOMAINS` tuple (order only affects Developer-Tools display order; the comment says put user-facing domains first and panel/setup/adapter last), and then `async_register_services` calls every `register(hass)` while `async_unregister_services` walks every `SERVICES` tuple calling `hass.services.async_remove(DOMAIN, name)`. There is NO per-module `remove()` hook — teardown is name-driven only, so a module cannot clean up anything else (see WIRE-5). Inside `register(hass)`, the body defines one thin `async def <service_name>(call: ServiceCall)` closure per service that forwards to a module-level `_handle_<name>(hass, call)`, then makes the `hass.services.async_register(DOMAIN, SERVICE_CONST, closure, schema=..., supports_response=...)` calls in a block at the bottom. The closure indirection exists so `hass` is captured without a partial; the `_handle_*` split exists so the handler is unit-testable without registration. Registration happens once per config entry, from `async_setup_entry` (`__init__.py:390`, `await async_register_services(hass)`), after `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME] = manager` is set at line 316 — so the manager is always present by the time a handler can run. Heavy subpackages are imported LAZILY inside `register()` (setup.py:131-139) or inside the handler (rooms.py:126-127, _common.py:71) to keep services-package import time clean. To add a 17th module: (1) add `SERVICE_*` constants to const.py; (2) create `services/<name>.py` with SERVICES + register + `_handle_*`; (3) import it in `services/__init__.py` and add it to `_DOMAINS`; (4) add a services.yaml block per service — this step is currently skipped 16 times (WIRE-3); (5) document it in docs/advanced/03-services.md.
notes.validation: All validation is voluptuous at the registration boundary; there is no post-schema validation layer. Schemas shared across domains live in `services/_common.py` — `VACUUM_ONLY_SCHEMA` ({Required vacuum_entity_id: cv.entity_id}), `VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA` (+ Optional map_id: cv.string), and `JOB_CONTROL_SCHEMA` which is literally `VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA` re-aliased. Everything else is a module-private `_UPPER_SNAKE_SCHEMA` defined at module scope above the handlers. Conventions actually followed: `vacuum_entity_id` is ALWAYS `vol.Required(...): cv.entity_id`; `map_id` is ALWAYS `vol.Optional(...): cv.string` (never cv.entity_id, and never Required except `reconcile_room`, rooms.py:74, where the map is the unit of the decision); ints are `vol.Coerce(int)` with `vol.Range` where a bound exists; enumerations are `vol.In([...])` inline (break_type, event_type, path_block_action, action, scope); lists are `vol.All(cv.ensure_list, [vol.Coerce(int)])`. Schemas are PREVENT_EXTRA by default, which is load-bearing: nearly every handler splats `**call.data` or `**resolved_call_data(hass, call)` straight into a manager method, so an unlisted key would be a TypeError. Custom validators are allowed and belong in the module — the one example is `_hex_color_or_none` (rooms.py:34-52), which canonicalises #rgb/#rrggbb, treats None/"" as an explicit clear, and raises `vol.Invalid` otherwise. Two things are trusted rather than validated: `set_maintenance_interval` deliberately does not clamp interval_hours (documented in its docstring: the card validates against the adapter's declared min/max first), and `_ZONE_RECT_SCHEMA` (job_control.py:115) deliberately does not range-clamp 0-1 because a drag to the image edge can land slightly outside and the provider clamps. One outright hole: `get_room_profiles` is registered with no schema at all (WIRE-4).
notes.errors: Three tiers, and which tier a handler uses is NOT consistent. (1) Raise nothing — the read-only getters (`get_queue_state`, `get_active_job`, `get_dashboard_snapshot`, `get_vacuum_maps`, all of access_graph) call the manager bare, so any exception propagates as-is; HA logs the traceback and the frontend shows a generic error. (2) `try/except Exception as err: raise HomeAssistantError(f"Failed to <verb>: {err}") from err` — the mutating/dispatching handlers (all of dock's actions, all of run_profiles, job_control's start/pause/resume/cancel/clear, rooms' discover/save/update/reconcile, maintenance). This is the dominant pattern and it does surface to the user, but the message body is a raw Python exception string, so a missing required kwarg reads as "Failed to cancel job: async_cancel_active_job() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'map_id'". (3) `ServiceValidationError` for a manager result that came back as a well-formed refusal — this is the important one and it is a strict post-check on the RETURNED payload, not on the input: `dock._check_dock_action` raises when `not payload.get('performed') and not payload.get('allowed', True)`; run_profiles raises when `not payload.get('<verb>ed') and payload.get('reason') == 'profile_not_found'` (five near-identical copies, lines 114, 133, 152, 171, plus set_run_profile_steps' `if not payload.get('saved')`); maintenance raises on `reason == 'no_source_entity'`. So: a manager refusal is only a user-visible error if the handler explicitly pattern-matches its reason code — anything else returns a success-shaped payload. NOTHING in this package catches broadly and returns a fabricated success; the swallow-shaped risk lives one layer down. Nothing is logged at WARNING/ERROR by handlers — every handler ends with `_LOGGER.debug("<name> complete: %s", payload)`, so the only trace of a refused-but-not-pattern-matched call is at DEBUG.
notes.responses: 57 of the 79 registrations declare `supports_response=True`. The ones that do NOT are, deliberately, the fire-and-forget mutators whose handler is typed `-> None`: `discover_rooms`, `save_managed_rooms`, `build_queue`, `build_room_payload`, `clear_queue`, `start_selected_rooms`, `clear_active_job`, plus `battery_rebaseline` (registered in __init__.py, not this package). There is NO envelope and no shared response builder — the returned dict is whatever the manager method returned, passed through unchanged, so the response contract is the manager's, not the service layer's. Three recurring shapes: (a) manager passthrough — `{...domain fields...}` with a boolean verb key (`updated`, `saved`, `applied`, `renamed`, `deleted`, `overwritten`, `cancelled`, `performed`, `reset`) plus a `reason` string on refusal; (b) status-envelope, used ONLY by services/setup.py — `{"status": "success"|"error", "message": str, ...}`, built by the handler itself; (c) hand-built payloads in errors.py/maintenance.py. Failure paths and success paths are distinguishable in most places but not all: `setup_save_rooms`, `setup_reject_rooms`, `setup_force_remove_room`, `setup_set_panel_title`, `setup_set_map_camera` all return `{"status": "error", "message": "Integration manager not available."}` when the manager is missing, which a caller CAN tell apart — but `setup_get_map_rooms` (setup.py:184) returns `{"rooms": [], "vacuum_entity_id": ..., "map_id": ...}` with no status key, and `errors.get_recent_errors` (errors.py:88-92) returns `{"errors": [], "reason": "tracker_not_loaded"}`. In both cases a caller that reads only the collection sees an empty list indistinguishable from a genuine empty result. If you add a service, pick shape (a) or (b) and make the not-loaded path carry a key the caller must read.
deviations: Manager access is bimodal. Ten modules use `_common.get_manager(hass)`, which is a bare `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]` subscript and raises KeyError when absent. services/setup.py and services/errors.py instead use `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_RUNTIME)` and return a graceful error shape. Neither uses `entry.runtime_data`, which __init__.py:317 populates and which is the idiomatic HA handle. Pick one; the graceful form is what the response contract above assumes.

Argument forwarding is bimodal. Most handlers splat (`manager.foo(**resolved_call_data(hass, call))`) — terse but it silently couples the schema key names to the manager signature. rooms.py:205-221 and setup.py:185-188/213-218/230-235 instead enumerate kwargs explicitly. The explicit form is the only one that can express intent like rooms.py:203's `color_kwargs = {'color': data['color']} if 'color' in data else {}` — passing the key ONLY when the caller supplied it, so "leave untouched" (absent) is distinguishable from "clear the override" (present, None). If your service has any tri-state field, you cannot use the splat.

map_id extraction after resolution is bimodal and one form can KeyError. rooms.py:207, setup.py:186-188/214/233 do `data['map_id']` on a schema where map_id is Optional — if auto-resolution failed the subscript raises KeyError. In rooms.py it is inside the try and becomes `HomeAssistantError("Failed to update room fields: 'map_id'")`; in setup.py it is NOT wrapped and propagates raw. setup.py:184 uses `data.get('map_id')` on one branch of the SAME handler that uses `data['map_id']` on the other.

Two handlers in services/setup.py reach into private manager internals: `setup_reject_rooms` calls `manager._notify_rooms_updated(...)` (line 253) and `setup_set_panel_title`/`setup_set_map_camera` mutate `manager.data['vacuums'][id]` dict entries directly (lines 299/301, 338/340) instead of going through a manager method. No other module does this.

`setup_add_vacuum` is the only handler with a side effect on the integration's own lifecycle: on `status == 'success'` it schedules `hass.config_entries.async_reload(...)` as a background task (setup.py:162-167). Any new service must assume a reload can begin while it is awaiting — which is exactly the exposure in WIRE-1.

The two `@debug_traceable` decorations are applied to the registration-time CLOSURE (job_control.py:282, 289), not to the `_handle_*` function. Only `start_selected_rooms` and `start_zone_clean` are flagged, so the debug flight recorder's default 'All flagged services' target arms exactly two of the 79 services.

`_common.job_finished_event_payload` / `run_incomplete_event_payload` intentionally duplicate `listeners/_common.job_finished_event_data` / `run_incomplete_event_data`. The docstrings say they are 'kept in sync'; they are not identical — the services-side pair accepts either a raw finalize result OR a `{'finalize_result': ...}` wrapper, the listeners-side pair accepts only the raw result. See WIRE-6.
gotchas: `resolved_call_data(hass, call)` returns a plain `dict(call.data)` with `map_id` INSERTED when it could be resolved and NOT inserted when it could not. It never raises and never inserts a placeholder. Its docstring promises the manager will raise on the missing kwarg — true for 44 of 46 entry points, false for `discover_rooms` (WIRE-2). If you add a service whose manager method defaults `map_id`, you own the missing-map behaviour yourself.

`get_active_map_id` is entity-existence-driven, not value-driven: present-and-blank (unknown/unavailable/none/null/empty) returns None deliberately rather than forking a second map; registered-but-stateless returns None; absent-from-both-state-machine-and-registry falls back to the adapter's implicit attribute map id. So auto-resolution failing is a NORMAL runtime condition during boot and cloud blips, not an edge case.

Almost no handler persists implicitly. The manager methods mutate `manager.data` in memory and the HANDLER is responsible for `await get_manager(hass).async_save()`. Some handlers make the save conditional on the result (`if result.get('updated')` in rooms.py:224, `if payload.get('reset')` in maintenance.py:70, `if payload.get('updated')` in dock.py:128) and some save unconditionally. If you forget the save, your mutation vanishes on restart with no error. Hold the manager in a local variable across any await instead of re-calling get_manager (WIRE-1).

Two handlers carry a MUST-NOT-EXECUTOR comment: `get_dashboard_snapshot` (snapshots.py:63-65) and `get_start_status` (job_control.py:139-142) call `hass.bus.async_fire` internally via `_maybe_roll_current_room_by_timing`, so they must stay on the event loop. Do not wrap a manager call in `async_add_executor_job` without checking whether it fires events.

Only `cancel_active_job` fires events from this package (`EVENT_JOB_FINISHED`, and `EVENT_RUN_INCOMPLETE` when the cancel stranded rooms). Every other lifecycle event is owned by `listeners/`. If you add a service that finalizes a job, you must fire both, and the run-incomplete builder returns None when nothing was missed so the caller skips the fire.

`services/debug.py` is not a normal domain module — it has no schemas or handlers of its own; `EUFY_AREAS` maps area names to logger-name SUBSTRINGS (e.g. 'dispatch' -> '.services.job_control', '.jobs', '.queue', ...). If you add a module whose logs should be capturable by area, add its dotted suffix there or the area filter silently drops it.
Service names in const.py are the wire contract for automations and for the Lovelace card. Renaming one is a breaking change with no deprecation shim anywhere in this package.

contract.area: JOB — job control and queue services (services/job_control.py, services/queue.py)

notes.pattern:
Every domain module exposes exactly two public names: `register(hass) -> None` and `SERVICES: tuple[str, ...]`. `services/__init__.py` lists the module in `_DOMAINS` (line 43) and calls `domain.register(hass)` on setup; teardown walks `domain.SERVICES` and calls `hass.services.async_remove(DOMAIN, name)`. Adding a 17th module means: create the file, add it to the `from . import (...)` block AND to `_DOMAINS`, and keep SERVICES one-for-one with your registrations (nothing verifies this — a name in SERVICES that was never registered, or a registration missing from SERVICES, both fail silently, the latter leaving the service alive after unload).

Inside a module the shape is a strict three-layer sandwich, followed in both audited files without exception:
  1. Module-private schemas at the top, named `_<SERVICE>_SCHEMA`. Shared ones (`VACUUM_ONLY_SCHEMA`, `VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA`, `JOB_CONTROL_SCHEMA`) are imported from `._common`. Note `JOB_CONTROL_SCHEMA = VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA` (_common.py:166) is a bare alias, not a distinct schema — pause/resume/cancel accept nothing beyond vacuum_entity_id + map_id even though `async_cancel_active_job` supports `forced_lifecycle_state`, `forced_lifecycle_message`, and `cancel_reason` (deliberately not exposed).
  2. Module-level `async def _handle_<service>(hass, call)` doing the actual work. This is where the manager call lives.
  3. A `register(hass)` function containing one thin closure per service (`async def <service>(call): return await _handle_<service>(hass, call)`) and then a block of `hass.services.async_register(...)` calls. The closures exist only to bind `hass`; putting logic in them breaks the pattern.

The manager is reached ONLY through `get_manager(hass)` (_common.py:35 — `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]`). It is called fresh each time, never cached in a local; `_handle_start_selected_rooms` calls it twice in four lines. Arguments are ALWAYS the full `**resolved_call_data(hass, call)` splat — no handler picks fields out of `call.data` by hand. The consequence you must respect: your manager method's keyword-only signature IS your service's parameter contract. A schema field the method does not accept is a TypeError at call time; a method parameter absent from the schema is unreachable.

`resolved_call_data(hass, call)` (_common.py:40) copies `call.data` and, when `map_id` is absent or blank AND `vacuum_entity_id` is present, fills it from `rooms.room_discovery.get_active_map_id(hass, vacuum_entity_id)` (which reads the adapter's declared `entities.active_map`). This is why every schema marks `map_id` Optional. It is a lazy import by design — do not hoist it, the rooms subpackage pulls adapter machinery the services package deliberately does not load at import time.

`@debug_traceable(SERVICE_NAME)` from `..debug_capture` decorates the closure (not the `_handle_` function). Only two of the twelve job_control services carry it and none of queue's do — see deviations.
notes.validation:
Voluptuous only, and shape-only. Style is `vol.Schema({vol.Required(...)/vol.Optional(...): <validator>})` with the implicit `extra=PREVENT_EXTRA`, so unknown keys are rejected — rely on that, do not add ALLOW_EXTRA.

The vocabulary in use:
  - entity ids: `cv.entity_id`. FORMAT ONLY — it does not check existence, integration ownership, or even domain. `light.kitchen` passes every schema in both modules. Nothing downstream re-checks it either; the queue break mutators will `ensure_map_bucket` a storage bucket for whatever you pass (JOB-8).
  - free text: `cv.string`. Accepts `""` — `profile_id: ""` clears the schema and is refused later by the manager, not here.
  - booleans: `cv.boolean`.
  - ints: `vol.All(vol.Coerce(int), vol.Range(min=..., max=...))`. Coerce FIRST, then Range — copy that order, a bare Range on a string fails confusingly.
  - enums: `vol.In([...])` with the literal list inline (`path_block_action`, `break_type`). There is no shared constant for these; the lists are hand-copied between sibling schemas, which is how `break_type` came to allow `zone` in one schema and not the other.
  - lists: `vol.All(cv.ensure_list, [<item schema>], vol.Length(min=1))` is the careful form (`zones`, job_control.py:123-124). The careless form is a bare `[cv.string]` / `[_ENTRY_SCHEMA]`, which ACCEPTS AN EMPTY LIST (`zone_ids`, `breaks`). Decide which you want and be explicit.

What is NOT enforced here, by convention: brand/device capability (that belongs at dispatch, where the adapter config is known — the `clean_times` comment at job_control.py:125-129 states this rule, though its specific claim is false for Eufy), room/zone/profile EXISTENCE (enforced at dispatch or by the manager returning a refusal dict), and CROSS-FIELD dependency. There is no cross-field validation anywhere in either module even where a field is logically required by another's value; the convention is to let the manager's normalizer drop the malformed entry and report it in the response. `vol.Any` is never used — if you need conditional requiredness you would be introducing it.

User input is trusted for identity (entity ids, map ids, profile ids, zone ids all reach storage unchecked) and distrusted for shape.
notes.errors:
Two incompatible conventions ship side by side, and this is the single most important thing to get right in a new module.

job_control.py's MUTATING handlers wrap the manager call:
    try:
        payload = await get_manager(hass).X(**resolved_call_data(hass, call))
    except Exception as err:
        raise HomeAssistantError(f"Failed to <verb>: {err}") from err
The user sees a red toast with the wrapped message; the original traceback is chained. Its READ-ONLY handlers (`get_start_status`, `get_active_job`, `get_job_progress_snapshot`, `get_job_control_state`, `get_lifecycle_state`) are deliberately unwrapped.

queue.py wraps NOTHING — all eleven handlers, mutating and read-only alike, let exceptions propagate raw. HA still surfaces the failure to the caller, but as an unclassified integration error with a full traceback.

`ServiceValidationError` is used ZERO times in the entire services package. Nothing distinguishes "you passed bad input" from "the integration broke" — every failure is an integration fault as far as HA is concerned. If you want a user-input error to read as one, you would be introducing that too (grep first; it may have landed elsewhere since).

The critical asymmetry: **a raise is the ONLY thing HA treats as failure. A refusal dict is not.** Almost nothing in these two modules raises on a refusal. The manager returns `{started: False}`, `{added: False}`, `{paused: False}`, `{cancelled: False}`, `{set: False}`, `{removed: False}` and the service call reports success. Whether the caller can even SEE that refusal depends entirely on supports_response.

Swallowing: `_handle_start_selected_rooms` and `_handle_clear_active_job` capture the manager's return into `payload`, log it at DEBUG, and return None. That local is the only place the refusal reason exists. Deeper down, `async_cancel_active_job` also swallows a finalizer exception on purpose (active_job.py:2266) so that a cancel always clears — deliberate, documented, and correct.

Persistence on failure: `await get_manager(hass).async_save()` is placed AFTER the try/except in every mutating handler, never in a `finally`. A raise therefore skips persistence while leaving the manager's in-place `self.data` mutations live in memory (JOB-7). If your new service mutates state before a step that can raise, this is the trap.
notes.responses:
`supports_response=True` is passed positionally-by-keyword in the `async_register` call and is the ONLY thing that makes the return value reachable. HA REJECTS `response_variable` / `returnResponse: true` against a service that lacks it — this is a hard error, not a silent None, which is why src/actions/rooms.js:55 carries an explicit rule about it.

Current state across the 23 audited services: 10 of 12 in job_control declare it (all but `start_selected_rooms` and `clear_active_job`); 8 of 11 in queue declare it (all but `build_queue`, `build_room_payload`, `clear_queue`). A handler that does not declare it must have return type `None` — the pattern holds, but it means the manager's return value is discarded, and in the two job_control cases that value is the only report of a refusal (JOB-1, JOB-3).

Guaranteed shapes, and how failure is discriminated from success — every one of these uses a distinct BOOLEAN key, which is the convention to follow:
  - start_run_profile: `{vacuum_entity_id, map_id, started: bool, reason, message, profile_id, profile}` — on success adds `warning`, `warning_message`, `active_job`, `learning_snapshot`; on `confirmation_required` adds `preflight` and `confirm_token`; on a profile-apply failure adds `applied_room_ids`, `missing_room_ids`. Discriminator: `started`.
  - start_zone_clean: success `{status: "dispatched", vacuum_entity_id, zone_count, clean_times}`. There is NO failure shape — every failure path in dispatch_zone_clean raises ValueError, which the handler converts to HomeAssistantError. This is the cleanest error contract in the two modules.
  - pause/resume/cancel: `{vacuum_entity_id, map_id, <paused|resumed|cancelled>: bool, reason, ...}`. Failure carries `active_job` (the untouched record) and reason `no_started_job` / `no_paused_job` / `no_active_job`; cancel's success carries `confirmed: bool` and `finalize_result` instead. Discriminator is the verb-boolean. Note cancel's `confirmed: False` means "we finalized after the 30s terminal-state timeout expired", NOT a failure — that is a second, independent signal.
  - queue break mutators: `{added|removed|set: bool}` merged with the FULL `get_queue_steps` payload (`{vacuum_entity_id, map_id, steps, breaks, has_breaks}`) via `**` spread on success. On the `added: False` / `removed: False` paths the steps payload is ABSENT — so the failure shape is a two-key dict, structurally different from success. `set_queue_breaks` is the exception: its `set: False` path DOES spread the steps payload, because that path also clears the store (see gotchas).
  - read-only getters: return the manager payload verbatim, always a dict, always including `vacuum_entity_id` and `map_id`. `get_start_status` is the important one — it is the only way to obtain a `confirm_token`.

Rule for a new service: if it can refuse, declare supports_response, and make the refusal shape structurally distinguishable from success by a boolean key — not by the absence of an optional field.
deviations: ERROR HANDLING SPLIT DOWN THE MIDDLE. job_control wraps its seven mutating handlers in `try/except Exception -> HomeAssistantError`; queue wraps none of its eleven. Same package, same call pattern, opposite conventions. Whichever you copy, you are following precedent — which is the problem. There is no documented rule.

`start_selected_rooms` IS THE ODD ONE OUT AMONG THE THREE START SERVICES. Its two siblings declare supports_response and return their refusal dict; it does not, so eleven distinct block reasons plus `confirmation_required` plus `vacuum_missing` are visible only at DEBUG. The docs (03-services.md:29) describe a response contract this service physically cannot honor. Do not treat it as the reference implementation for a new start service — `start_run_profile` is.

`start_zone_clean` BYPASSES THE PREFLIGHT ENTIRELY. The other two start services route through `get_start_status` before touching the robot; this one calls `manager.dispatch_zone_clean` directly. It is the only service in either module that commands the device with no lifecycle, active-job, or vacuum-state check.

`clear_active_job` IS THE ONLY DESTRUCTIVE SERVICE WITH NO PRECONDITION. Its lifecycle siblings all gate on job status before acting; it overwrites the record unconditionally, persists immediately, and returns nothing.

`strict_order` EXISTS ON start_selected_rooms BUT NOT ON start_run_profile. Deliberate — a stepped profile is forced into strict order by the plan builder — but it means the two start schemas are near-twins with one unexplained field difference, and the reason lives in docs (03-services.md:195), not in the code.

`@debug_traceable` IS ON 2 OF 23. Only `start_selected_rooms` and `start_zone_clean` carry it. `start_run_profile` — which the docs call "the recommended way to launch a named preset from an automation" — does not, and because it invokes `manager.start_selected_rooms` directly rather than the service, it does not inherit the other decorator either. The debug flight recorder has a blind spot on the recommended automation path. No queue service is traced at all.

THREE DIFFERENTLY-SHAPED WRITE PATHS INTO ONE STORE. `queue_breaks` is written by `add_queue_break` (`{break_type, after_index, target_battery_percent?, wait_minutes?}`), `add_queue_zone` (`{after_index, zone_ids}`), and `set_queue_breaks` (a list of a fourth shape). It is READ back by `get_queue_steps` in a fifth shape (`{after_index, step}`) that none of the writers accept. The break-type vocabulary is hand-copied between two schemas and has already diverged (`zone` is in `_QUEUE_BREAK_ENTRY_SCHEMA`, not in `_ADD_QUEUE_BREAK_SCHEMA`).

`build_queue` / `build_room_payload` / `clear_queue` DISCARD THEIR PAYLOAD with no supports_response, unlike the eight other queue services. Recoverable via the `get_queue_state` / `get_payload_state` getters, so this is a wart rather than the JOB-1 problem — but it is the same shape of decision.
gotchas: THE HANDLER'S RETURN VALUE IS INERT WITHOUT `supports_response=True`. Adding a rich response dict to a handler changes nothing user-visible until you add that flag to the registration — and adding the flag later is a breaking change for anyone whose YAML relied on it being absent. Decide at creation.
A REFUSAL DICT IS NOT AN ERROR. `{"started": False}` completes the service call successfully. If the user must know, you have to raise. There is no middle setting.

PUT `async_save()` IN A `finally` (OR SAVE BEFORE ANY STEP THAT CAN RAISE) IF YOUR SERVICE MUTATES BEFORE IT CAN FAIL. The existing pattern places it after the try/except, which loses persistence of already-applied mutations on the failure path.

`set_queue_breaks` DESTROYS THE STORE ON ITS FAILURE PATH. With fewer than two enabled rooms it sets `map_bucket["queue_breaks"] = []` and THEN returns `{"set": False, "reason": "needs_two_rooms"}` (core/manager.py:1809-1820). A response that reads as "nothing happened" has in fact deleted every stored break, and the handler persists it. Documented in the manager docstring, invisible from the response.

`_QUEUE_BREAK_ENTRY_SCHEMA` SILENTLY DROPS ENTRIES IT ACCEPTS. An entry that clears the schema but fails `normalize_run_profile_steps` (a `wait` with no `wait_minutes`, a `zone` with no `zone_ids`) is `continue`d out of the wholesale replace, and the response still says `"set": True`. The user's list is silently shorter than what they sent.

AN ENTITY ID IS NOT VALIDATED BEYOND ITS SPELLING. If your service writes to storage keyed by `vacuum_entity_id`, a typo creates a permanent phantom bucket. `get_map_bucket` (non-creating) and `ensure_map_bucket` (creating) are both in use in this package — pick the non-creating one on any path that might be reached with an unverified id.

A COMMENT DEFERRING A CHECK TO ANOTHER LAYER MUST NAME THE BRANCH. `clean_times` has no upper bound because a comment says dispatch enforces the per-brand ceiling; dispatch does — inside the `zone_coords == "device_mm"` branch only, so Eufy gets no clamp at all (JOB-4). If you defer validation, verify the deferred-to code covers BOTH shipped brands, not just the one you were looking at.

A PHASED (strict_order) JOB HAS AN AWAIT-GAP HAZARD ON CANCEL. `async_cancel_active_job` writes `_cancel_in_flight = True` and `_phase_dispatch_pending = False` into the stored record (active_job.py:2203-2208) BEFORE awaiting `vacuum.return_to_base`. If that service call raises, the handler converts it to HomeAssistantError, `async_save()` never runs, and the job is left `started` with its phase watchdog disarmed and cancel latched — the run cannot advance until a later cancel succeeds. Roborock-only (Eufy jobs are atomic and carry no `phases`). Any new service that pre-writes state before awaiting a device command inherits this shape.

SERVICE HANDLERS ARE ASYNC AND DO AWAIT. State read before an `await` may be stale after it. `_handle_cancel_active_job` reads `resolved_call_data` once into a local and reuses it across the manager await for the event payloads — correct, because it is call input rather than manager state. Do not read manager state before an await and act on it after.

`get_start_status` MUST STAY ON THE EVENT LOOP. It fires `hass.bus.async_fire` internally via `_build_effective_start_plan -> _maybe_roll_current_room_by_timing`. The docstring at job_control.py:139-143 explicitly forbids `async_add_executor_job` for it. The inverse rule also ships: `start_selected_rooms` offloads its snapshot write with `hass.async_add_executor_job` (manager.py:5121) because that path does disk I/O. Know which side of the line your manager method is on before you pick.

THE SERVICE'S PARAMETER CONTRACT IS THE MANAGER METHOD'S SIGNATURE, because of the `**resolved_call_data(...)` splat. Adding a schema field without adding the keyword to the manager method is a TypeError at call time; the reverse is dead config. There is no adapter/mapping layer between them.

contract.area: ROOMS — room and profile mutation (services/rooms.py, services/room_profiles.py, services/access_graph.py)

notes.pattern: Every module in the package exposes exactly two names: `SERVICES: tuple[str, ...]` (the const names it registers) and `register(hass) -> None`. services/__init__.py holds an ordered `_DOMAINS` tuple, calls every module's register() on setup and walks every module's SERVICES on teardown — adding a 17th module means importing it in that tuple, nothing else. Inside a module the shape is: module-level `_<NAME>_SCHEMA` voluptuous constants; module-level `async def _handle_<name>(hass, call)` functions holding the logic; and inside register(), one thin `async def <name>(call)` closure per service that captures hass and forwards to its _handle_ function, then one async_register call per service. room_profiles.py is the outlier that inlines nothing but still keeps the closure layer, so the closures are pure boilerplate there. The manager is reached ONLY through `get_manager(hass)` from services/_common.py, which is a bare `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]` with no None handling — services/setup.py uses `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_RUNTIME)` with an explicit None branch instead, so there are two competing manager accessors in the package. map_id is resolved through `resolved_call_data(hass, call)` from _common.py, which returns `dict(call.data)` with map_id filled from the adapter's declared active_map entity when the caller omitted it or passed a blank string; it returns the data UNCHANGED when the vacuum_entity_id is missing or no active_map entity exists. Handlers that take map_id must use it; handlers that do not (get_vacuum_maps, get_room_profiles, the four profile-library services) use `call.data` directly. Mutations end with `await get_manager(hass).async_save()` — persistence is the HANDLER's job, never the manager's; the manager mutates `self.data` in place and returns.
notes.validation: Voluptuous only, at the schema constant, with `cv` helpers. Every schema is a bare `vol.Schema({...})`, so PREVENT_EXTRA is in force — an unlisted key fails the whole call with `extra keys not allowed @ data['<key>']`. The idioms in use: `vol.Required('vacuum_entity_id'): cv.entity_id`; `vol.Optional('map_id'): cv.string` (optional everywhere except reconcile_room, which requires it because migrate is destructive); `vol.Required('room_id'): vol.Coerce(int)`; list fields as `vol.All(cv.ensure_list, [vol.Coerce(int)])`; enums as `vol.In([...])` (only reconcile_room's `action` uses this). Three shared schemas live in _common.py — VACUUM_ONLY_SCHEMA, VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA, and JOB_CONTROL_SCHEMA which is literally `= VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA`; access_graph.py reuses VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA for get_access_graph_health while every other map-scoped schema in the area re-declares the same two keys inline. What is actually ENFORCED at the boundary: entity-id syntax (not existence — an entity_id belonging to another integration's vacuum, or to no entity at all, passes), integer coercibility, and hex-colour canonicality (`_hex_color_or_none`, services/rooms.py:34-52, the only custom validator in the area and the only one that raises vol.Invalid). What is NOT enforced anywhere: the cleaning vocabulary. clean_mode / fan_speed / water_level / clean_intensity are `cv.string` on both update_room_fields and the two explicit-field profile services, even though the adapter declares the legal sets (`dispatch.global_pre_calls[].rank`, adapters/roborock/vocabulary.py). Numeric ranges are not enforced either — clean_passes is a bare Coerce(int) (it is clamped later at queue/queue_engine.py:294, so it is denormalised in storage but safe on the wire); room ids are not checked for existence; grants_access_to targets are not checked against the map's rooms. The rule is: the schema checks TYPE, the manager-side normalisers (_normalize_grants_access_to, _normalize_room_rules, normalize_room_profile) check SHAPE, and nothing checks VOCABULARY. A new module should assume user input is trusted for meaning and only distrusted for form.
notes.errors: Two mechanisms, applied inconsistently. (1) `try: ... except Exception as err: raise HomeAssistantError(f'Failed to <verb>: {err}') from err` — used by 4 of 5 handlers in rooms.py (all but get_vacuum_maps) and by 0 of 8 in room_profiles.py and 0 of 2 in access_graph.py. HA renders a HomeAssistantError as a toast with that message and no traceback; an unwrapped exception becomes an 'Error executing service' log entry plus a generic failure to the caller. (2) `vol.Invalid` raised from a custom schema validator — only _hex_color_or_none does this — which HA converts to a ServiceValidationError shown to the user with the validator's message. `ServiceValidationError` is never raised directly anywhere in this area. Everything else is a RETURN VALUE, not an exception: 'room not found', 'profile not found', 'profile name exists', 'protected profile', 'missing label', 'invalid access graph' are all success-status service calls carrying a failure payload. The practical rule for a new module: a bad ARGUMENT should raise (schema or HomeAssistantError); a bad STATE should return a failure payload. Note the gap this leaves — a missing map_id after auto-resolve failure is neither: it becomes a KeyError or a TypeError from the manager splat, which reads as a bug rather than as 'you have no active map configured'.
notes.responses: supports_response=True is declared for every service that returns data and for every mutation EXCEPT save_managed_rooms and discover_rooms, both of which are registered plain and whose handlers are annotated `-> None` and discard the manager's payload. All 8 room-profile services and both access-graph services declare it. There is no single response envelope; each family has its own boolean verb key plus a `reason` string on failure, and the success and failure shapes are NOT the same object with a flag — they are different key sets, which is what a caller must branch on. The shapes actually returned: update_room_fields -> `{'ok': True, vacuum_entity_id, map_id, room_id, 'updated': True, 'profile_name', 'room': {...}}` on success, `{'ok': False, 'updated': False, 'error': 'room_not_found'|'invalid_access_graph', 'reason', 'reason_detail', 'issues': [...]}` on failure — the only service in the area with a consistent `ok` flag on both arms, and the model to copy. reconcile_room -> `{vacuum_entity_id, map_id, action, migrated_room_count, id_remap: {old_str: new_int}, dropped: [slug,...]}` plus `'skipped': 'no_discovery'` when it refused. save_user_room_profile -> `{'saved': bool, 'profile_name', 'profile'}` with `'reason'` + `'message'` added when saved is False. overwrite_room_profile -> `{'overwritten': bool, ...}`; rename -> `{'renamed': bool, 'previous_profile_name', ...}`; delete -> `{'deleted': bool, ...}`; the from_room variants add vacuum_entity_id/map_id/room_id to all arms. Reason strings in use: protected_profile, profile_not_found, profile_name_exists, missing_label, room_not_found, room_details_unavailable, no_discovery, invalid_access_graph. apply_room_profile is the one that breaks the pattern — it has NO boolean verb key at all, returns `{updated_room_ids, room_count}` on success and `{error: 'profile_not_found', updated_room_ids: []}` on the only failure it reports, and reports nothing for unknown room ids (ROOMS-5). get_room_access_editor and get_access_graph_health are pure reads and return a `reason: 'room_not_found'` key instead of raising. A new module should return a boolean verb key on BOTH arms and a `reason` slug on the failure arm, and must not rely on the absence of an `error` key meaning success.
deviations: reconcile_room is the only service in the area where map_id is vol.Required rather than auto-resolved — deliberate, because migrate is destructive, and documented as such in docs/advanced/03-services.md:274.
get_room_profiles is registered with NO schema at all (services/room_profiles.py:203-205), so any payload is accepted and ignored. Every other service in the area has one.
get_vacuum_maps is the only handler in rooms.py without a try/except, and the only one that uses `**call.data` instead of resolved_call_data (correct — it takes no map_id).
save_managed_rooms and discover_rooms are the only services in the area without supports_response; save_managed_rooms is also the most destructive, so the area's riskiest call is its most silent one.

services/rooms.py wraps its manager calls in HomeAssistantError; services/room_profiles.py and services/access_graph.py do not wrap any of theirs. Same package, same failure modes, opposite treatment.

_handle_save_managed_rooms and every handler in room_profiles.py call `get_manager(hass)` TWICE — once for the operation and once for `async_save()` — where rooms.py's other handlers bind it to a local first. Harmless but it is two idioms for one thing.

_hex_color_or_none rejects a bad value at the boundary with vol.Invalid; the four cleaning-vocabulary fields in the same schema accept anything. The schema demonstrates the right pattern and then does not apply it to the fields that reach the robot.

services.yaml and the voluptuous schemas have drifted apart for three services in this area (save_managed_rooms declares floor_types + carpet_types; save_user_room_profile and overwrite_room_profile declare a required `carpet`) — all four fields are rejected by PREVENT_EXTRA. services.yaml is a DOC, not a validator; the schema is the only thing HA enforces, and nothing in CI diffs them.

apply_room_profile and update_room_fields call ensure_map_bucket, which CREATES a durable empty map bucket for an unknown map_id; get_managed_rooms / get_effective_room_details call get_map_bucket, which returns an ephemeral empty shape instead. Read paths do not create, two write paths do, and neither validates the id first.
gotchas: `cv.ensure_list(None)` returns `[]`, so `vol.Optional('x'): vol.All(cv.ensure_list, [...])` DESTROYS the omitted-vs-null distinction before your handler ever sees it. If a downstream function branches on `is not None` (build_managed_rooms does, room_manager.py:53) that branch is already dead for a null input. Either accept the collapse deliberately or validate `vol.Length(min=1)`.

Handlers own persistence. If you forget `await manager.async_save()` your mutation survives until the next restart and then silently reverts. Conversely, save unconditionally and you persist no-op writes; update_room_fields gates on `result.get('updated')` and that is the better pattern.

The whole `data` dict is persisted verbatim by core/storage.py — including `data['discovery']`, which is a CACHE that outlives restarts and can be arbitrarily stale. Anything that rebuilds from it (save_managed_rooms, reconcile_room, rebuild_map) is rebuilding from possibly-ancient state. reconcile_room guards the empty case; save_managed_rooms does not.

The discovery cache is keyed by the vacuum's ACTIVE map (`payload['active_map_id']`), not by the map_id you asked for. Any service that reads `data['discovery'][vac][map_id]` for a non-active map gets `{}`.

Handlers are async and DO await between reads and writes — `async_refresh_room_source`, `async_save`, and every service the dispatch layer calls. A read-modify-write that spans an await is NOT atomic. The one place this is done right is update_room_fields' snapshot/validate/rollback block, which is entirely synchronous.

A `map_id` that cannot be auto-resolved does not produce a clean error: `data['map_id']` KeyErrors or the `**data` splat TypeErrors. If your handler needs map_id, either read it as `data['map_id']` inside a try that raises HomeAssistantError, or check for it and return a `{'reason': 'no_active_map'}` payload — do not rely on the manager to explain itself.

Voluptuous PREVENT_EXTRA means adding a field to services.yaml is NOT enough — you must add it to the schema too, or the form HA renders becomes uncallable. Three services in this area already have this bug.

'Room id' is spelled three ways in this area: `_safe_int(r, -1) >= 0` (apply_room_profile, admits 0), `> 0` (_normalize_grants_access_to, normalize_run_profile_steps), and `int(room['room_id'])` with no guard (build_managed_rooms). Pick `> 0` — 0 is not a real segment id on either shipped brand.

Mutating room settings mid-run does NOT change what a running job dispatches: phases carry their own `resolved_rooms` and `payload` snapshots taken at start (jobs/phase_runner.py:1010-1023). No service in this area refuses a mutation while a job is running, and none needs to for dispatch reasons — but nothing stops save_managed_rooms from emptying the room store under a running job, which does affect slug-based live id resolution and finalisation.

`profile_name` on a room is a soft reference with no integrity: an unknown name resolves silently to the catalog's default_profile ('vacuum_quick') at profiles/room_profiles.py:284-289. Never treat a room's profile_name as proof the profile exists.

The framework's mop test is spelled two incompatible ways — case-insensitive substring (`'mop' in clean_mode.lower()`, profiles/manager.py:96 and dispatch/manager.py:381) on the storage/UI side, exact-match set (`clean_mode in {'mop','vacuum_mop'}`, queue/queue_engine.py:302/305 and profiles/room_profiles.py:505) on the payload side. Any service that lets a user write clean_mode freely can land a value that reads as mopping in one layer and as not-mopping in the other.

contract.area: AREA 4 — SETUP, ONBOARDING AND ADAPTER CONFIG (services/setup.py, services/adapter_config.py)

notes.pattern: Each domain module exposes exactly two public names — `register(hass) -> None` and `SERVICES: tuple[str, ...]` — and `services/__init__.py` calls every module's `register` on setup (`async_register_services`) and walks every module's `SERVICES` on teardown (`async_unregister_services`, which does `hass.services.async_remove(DOMAIN, name)` per entry). Adding a 17th module means: create `services/<name>.py`, define `SERVICES`, define `register`, and add the module to both the import list and the `_DOMAINS` tuple in `services/__init__.py:22-57`. Ordering in `_DOMAINS` is cosmetic only (Developer Tools display order). Service NAME constants live in `const.py` (SERVICE_* ), never as literals in the module. Schemas are module-private `_UPPER_SNAKE_SCHEMA` names defined at module scope, except the three genuinely shared ones — `VACUUM_ONLY_SCHEMA`, `VACUUM_MAP_SCHEMA`, `JOB_CONTROL_SCHEMA` — which live in `services/_common.py`. Two registration styles coexist: setup.py defines every handler as a closure INSIDE `register()` (which is also where its heavy `..setup.*` imports live, deliberately lazy to keep the services package import-time clean — see the comment at setup.py:128), while adapter_config.py defines module-level `async def _handle_<name>(hass, call)` functions and wraps each in a trivial closure inside `register()`. adapter_config.py's style is the better one (testable without a hass fixture); setup.py's is the larger module. Whichever you pick, keep it consistent within the file. Manager access has two forms and they are NOT interchangeable: `_common.get_manager(hass)` does a bare `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]` and RAISES KeyError when the integration is not loaded; the tolerant form is `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_RUNTIME)` followed by an explicit `if manager is None:` branch. Both appear inside adapter_config.py. Any handler that mutates `manager.data` must `await manager.async_save()` itself — the manager does not autosave, and the helpers in setup/ and rooms/ are pure data mutators that explicitly document 'the caller is responsible for calling manager.async_save()'.
notes.validation: Voluptuous schemas are the ONLY declarative validation layer, and they stop at type. `cv.entity_id` on `vacuum_entity_id` validates SHAPE (domain.object_id), never existence, never that the entity belongs to a vacuum this integration manages, never that it is a vacuum at all — a caller can pass `light.kitchen` to any service in this area. Exactly one handler in the area closes that gap: `setup/workflow.add_vacuum` checks `hass.states.get(vacuum_entity_id) is None` and returns status 'blocked'. Every other handler either checks membership in `manager.data['vacuums']` (setup_set_panel_title, setup_set_map_camera, import_active_map) or checks nothing at all (setup_save_rooms, setup_reject_rooms, setup_force_remove_room, setup_delete_map, and all six adapter-config services). All schemas are default PREVENT_EXTRA — there is no `extra=vol.ALLOW_EXTRA` in the package — so a typo'd field name raises vol.Invalid, which is the one thing the validation layer reliably catches. `map_id` is `vol.Optional(...): cv.string` on every service that takes one; `_common.resolved_call_data(hass, call)` returns a COPY of call.data with map_id filled in from `rooms.room_discovery.get_active_map_id`, and returns it UNCHANGED when it cannot resolve — so after calling it you must use `data.get('map_id')`, never `data['map_id']`. Closed value sets are enforced NOWHERE at the service boundary: floor types (canonical set at profiles/room_profiles.py:257), setup step ids (SETUP_STEP_IDS at setup/drift.py:54), dispatch templates (queue/dispatch_engines.known_dispatch_templates), adapter-config shape (adapters/config_schema.ADAPTER_CONFIG_SCHEMA) — every one of these is either clamped silently at read time or checked only in the test suite. ADAPTER_CONFIG_SCHEMA in particular declares `adapter_id`, `source`, `entities` and `dispatch` as required and is imported by nothing outside tests/adapters/test_adapter_contract.py; `save_adapter_config` applies two ad-hoc presence checks instead. `registry._validate_adapter` is the closest thing to runtime adapter validation and it is advisory only: it returns a list of issue strings that `register_adapter_config` logs at WARNING and then ignores, raising only TypeError for a non-dict. It also only inspects blocks that are PRESENT — an omitted block produces no issue, by design (`_warn_eufy_fallbacks` logs an advisory for the three engine blocks and is explicitly documented as 'deliberately not an entry in the validation issues list').
notes.errors: Neither audited module contains a single `try`, `except`, `raise`, `HomeAssistantError` or `ServiceValidationError` — verified by grep. That is 18 services, including the two most destructive in the integration, with no typed error path. The consequences are threefold. (1) Anything that raises inside a handler escapes as its raw exception type: `data['map_id']` on an unresolved map produces a bare `KeyError: 'map_id'` with a traceback in the log, not an HA-shaped error. (2) Every anticipated failure is instead encoded IN THE RESPONSE BODY as `{'status': 'error'|'blocked'|'requires_confirmation'|'already_done', ...}`, so the service call itself always reports success to HA — an automation cannot use error handling, it must inspect `response_variable`. (3) The two services with no supports_response at all (save_adapter_config, delete_adapter_config) have no channel whatsoever: their failure paths `_LOGGER.error(...)` and `return`. The in-repo reference for the pattern this area is missing is `services/rooms.py:222` — `except Exception as err: raise HomeAssistantError(f'Failed to update room fields: {err}') from err` — and five sibling modules (dock, job_control, maintenance, rooms, run_profiles) do raise typed HA errors. A new module should follow rooms.py, not setup.py: raise ServiceValidationError for bad user input, HomeAssistantError for an operation that failed, and reserve the status-in-body shape for outcomes that are legitimately non-error (already_done, requires_confirmation).

The closures exist only to bind `hass`; all logic lives in the `_handle_*` functions so tests can call them directly. Argument passing is always `manager.method(**resolved_call_data(hass, call))` — kwargs splat straight from the validated ServiceCall data into a keyword-only manager signature, so a schema key and a manager parameter name are the SAME identifier and renaming either one silently breaks the other with a TypeError at call time.
