notes.errors: The package convention is: wrap the manager call in `try: payload = manager.x(**resolved_call_data(hass, call)) except Exception as err: raise HomeAssistantError(f"Failed to <verb>: {err}") from err`, then inspect the returned payload and `raise ServiceValidationError(...)` for the user-error cases. `ServiceValidationError` is the class to use for anything the user can fix (unknown profile_id, bad steps); `HomeAssistantError` for internal failures. Both are shown in the HA UI; a bare exception is not (it lands in the log as 'Error executing service'). The rule that is NOT followed consistently and is the single biggest hazard in this area: the payload inspection is written as a REASON-LITERAL match, not a flag check. Five of the seven run-profile handlers read `if not payload.get(<verb_flag>) and payload.get("reason") == "profile_not_found"`, so every OTHER failure reason the manager can return (`no_rooms_selected`, `missing_name`, or no reason key at all) falls through the gate, gets persisted by the trailing `async_save()`, and is returned to the caller as a success. `_handle_set_run_profile_steps` shows the correct form — `if not payload.get("saved"): raise ServiceValidationError(f"...: {payload.get('reason', 'unknown')}")` — and `_handle_save_run_profile` shows the worst form: no inspection at all. A new module MUST gate on the flag and pass the reason through, never on a reason literal. Read-only handlers (`_handle_get_saved_run_profiles`, `_handle_get_dashboard_snapshot`, `_handle_get_upkeep_snapshot`, `_handle_get_pause_timeout_settings`) skip the try/except entirely, which is the module's own deviation, not a rule. Every handler ends with `_LOGGER.debug("<service> complete: %s", payload)`; failures are logged at debug too, so nothing in this area is visible at default log level.
notes.responses: All 11 services in this area register with `supports_response=True` and return a plain dict — never None, never a dataclass. There is no `ServiceResponse` typing and no shared response builder. Every response echoes its inputs: `{"vacuum_entity_id": ..., "map_id": str(map_id), ...}`. Mutating run-profile services carry a per-service BOOLEAN VERB FLAG plus, on failure, a `reason` string — `save_run_profile` -> `{"saved": bool, "profile_id": str, "profile": {...}}` / `{"saved": False, "reason": "missing_name"|"no_rooms_selected"}`; `set_run_profile_steps` -> `{"saved": ...}` / reason `"profile_not_found"|"no_room_group"`; `apply_run_profile` -> `{"applied": bool, "profile_id", "profile", "applied_room_ids": [int], "missing_room_ids": [int]}` / reason `"profile_not_found"`; `overwrite_run_profile` -> `{"overwritten": bool, ...}`; `rename_run_profile` -> `{"renamed": bool, ...}`; `delete_run_profile` -> `{"deleted": bool, "profile_id"}` (no `profile` echo on success — the only mutator that omits it). `get_saved_run_profiles` returns `{"profile_count": int, "profiles": [ {id,name,room_count,room_ids,room_names,room_names_label,expose_as_button,created_at,updated_at,summary} ], "library": {profile_id: <enriched profile>}}` — i.e. the same data twice, a sorted lightweight list and an id-keyed enriched map. The kwargs splat means a schema key IS a manager parameter name. The card is not a safety net. `src/actions/core.js` only toasts on a raised exception, and the run-profile bindings check `result?.ok === false` — a key these services never return. If your handler does not RAISE, no user anywhere sees the failure.

Every service module in this package follows the same four-part shape, and all three audited modules obey it.

(1) Module-level `SERVICES: tuple[str, ...]` of const names, and `def register(hass: HomeAssistant) -> None`. `services/__init__.py` calls every module's `register` on setup and walks every module's `SERVICES` on teardown (documented at services/_common.py:16-19). A 17th module must export both or it will register but never unregister.

(2) Inside `register`, one thin `async def <name>(call: ServiceCall) -> dict` closure per service that does nothing but `return await _handle_<name>(hass, call)`. The closure exists solely to bind `hass`; ALL logic lives in a module-level `_handle_*` coroutine taking `(hass, call)`. errors.py is the one module that skips the `_handle_*`/closure split for nothing — it still has both. Follow the split: the `_handle_*` functions are what the tests import directly (see tests/integration/test_services_dock.py, which calls `_handle_wash_mop` with a stubbed manager).

(3) `hass.services.async_register(DOMAIN, SERVICE_<NAME>, <closure>, schema=..., supports_response=True)`. Every one of the ten registrations in these three modules passes `supports_response=True`. Service name constants live in `../const`; the schema is either a shared one from `_common` or a module-private `_<NAME>_SCHEMA` defined at the top of the file. `_common` docstring states the rule: "Schemas that are genuinely shared across domains — VACUUM_ONLY, VACUUM_MAP, JOB_CONTROL. Domain-specific schemas live with their domain."

(4) Resolving the target. Two helpers, both in `services/_common.py`:
  - `get_manager(hass)` -> `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]`. Note the BARE subscript: it raises KeyError if the manager is absent. services/setup.py instead uses `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_RUNTIME)` plus a None check returning `{"status": "error", ...}`; errors.py uses a third form, `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_ERROR_TRACKER)` with a None check returning `{"acknowledged": False, "reason": "tracker_not_loaded"}`. Three shapes for the same question.
  - `resolved_call_data(hass, call)` -> `dict(call.data)` with `map_id` filled in from `rooms.room_discovery.get_active_map_id` when the caller omitted it. Use this for ANY service taking a map_id; `**`-splat the result into the manager method. dock.py uses it for the five map-taking services and correctly does NOT use it for `set_dock_event_count` (dock events are per-device). errors.py and maintenance.py take no map_id and splat `**call.data` directly.

Handlers do not talk to devices. They splat into a `EufyVacuumManager` method which is almost always a one-line `**kwargs` delegator to a subsystem manager (`self.dock`, `self.maintenance`) — see core/manager.py:981-1003. The subsystem method owns the gating, the storage write, and the response dict; the service handler owns validation escalation, logging, and the `async_save()` call.

Four distinct behaviours, mapped to what HA shows the user:

1. `ServiceValidationError(msg)` -> HA shows `msg` verbatim to the user as a red service error. Use for "your input was wrong" and for a gated action the user could unblock. Used by `_check_dock_action` and by `_handle_reset_maintenance`'s no_source_entity branch. This is the only error type in these modules whose text is written for a human.

2. `except Exception as err: raise HomeAssistantError(f"Failed to X: {err}") from err` -> HA shows "Failed to X: <python repr>". This is the house style for wrapping a manager call. Present on all four dock actions, on `set_dock_event_count`, on `reset_maintenance`, and on `set_maintenance_interval`'s storage write. It catches bare `Exception`, so a `TypeError` from a bad splat gets dressed up as a plausible-looking failure message with a Python signature as its body.

3. Unwrapped — the exception reaches HA raw and is logged as an unhandled service error with a traceback. `_handle_get_dock_action_status` (the only dock handler with no try/except) and BOTH errors.py handlers are in this bucket. notes.responses:
All ten services declare `supports_response=True` and every success path returns a dict. There is NO shared response envelope — each domain invented its own success key, and none of them is `status`:

  dock, gated actions (`wash_mop`/`dry_mop`/`empty_dust`/`stop_dry_mop`) — success: `{"vacuum_entity_id", "map_id" (str-coerced), "action", "performed": True, "allowed": True, "reason": "performed", "message": "Dock action sent.", "entity_id", "dock_status", "lifecycle_state"}`. The blocked shape (`performed: False, allowed: False, reason: <gate>, message: <human>`, NO `entity_id` key) is built by the manager but the SERVICE never returns it — `_check_dock_action` turns it into a ServiceValidationError. So from a caller's perspective these four services return exactly one shape or raise. `performed` and `allowed` are literals set by `_async_run_dock_action`, not observations: they say "we called button.press", not "the dock did anything".

  dock, `get_dock_action_status` — `{"vacuum_entity_id", "map_id", "docked", "dock_status", "dock_status_label", "lifecycle_state", "lifecycle_state_label", "lifecycle_message", "active_job_status", "active_job_status_label", "actions": {<4 action keys>: {"supported", "entity_id", "allowed", "reason", "reason_label", "message"}}, "can_wash_mop", "can_dry_mop", "can_stop_dry_mop", "can_empty_dust", "updated_at"}`. `can_*` are convenience mirrors of `actions[x]["allowed"]`. The `*_label` fields come from `_display_label` (underscores to spaces, Title Case) and are NOT i18n-routed.

  dock, `set_dock_event_count` — success: `{"updated": True, "event_type", "old_count", "new_count"}`. Note it does NOT echo `vacuum_entity_id`. `old_count` is the ONLY record of the destroyed value anywhere in the system. The manager's failure shape `{"updated": False, "error": "Unknown event_type: ..."}` is unreachable through the service (the schema's `vol.In` already rejects it).

  maintenance, `reset_maintenance` — success: `{"vacuum_entity_id", "component", "reset": True, "reset_at_usage_hours", "reset_at", "source_entity"}`. Failure shapes DO reach the caller for two of three reasons: `{"reset": False, "reason": "source_unavailable", "source_entity"}` and `{"reset": False, "reason": "invalid_usage_hours", "source_entity"}` are returned as-is; only `no_source_entity` is escalated to an exception. So a caller must handle BOTH a raised error and a `reset: False` dict.

  maintenance, `set_maintenance_interval` — `{"saved": True, "vacuum_entity_id", "component", "interval_hours"}`. There is no `saved: False` path: the dict is constructed unconditionally after the try, so `saved` is a constant, not a result. It reports what was written, never whether the component was real.

  errors, `acknowledge_error` — `{"acknowledged": bool, "vacuum_entity_id", "scope"}` OR, on the tracker-missing path only, `{"acknowledged": False, "reason": "tracker_not_loaded"}` — note that shape drops `vacuum_entity_id` and `scope`, and that `reason` is present on ONE of the two false paths. `acknowledged: True` means "an error_tracker record existed for this vacuum", not "a latch was cleared", and it does not distinguish a deleted latch from a mid-run MARKED-and-retained one.

  errors, `get_recent_errors` — success: `{"vacuum_entity_id", "errors": [...], "count": len(errors)}`; tracker-missing: `{"vacuum_entity_id", "errors": [], "reason": "tracker_not_loaded"}` — same keys minus `count`, plus `reason`. A caller reading `count` unconditionally KeyErrors on the failure path.

Rule for a 17th module: pick the existing success key of the closest sibling, always echo `vacuum_entity_id`, and make the failure shape a SUPERSET of the success shape (same keys plus `reason`) rather than a different one — every failure shape in these three modules today drops keys the success shape has.
deviations: `_handle_get_dock_action_status` is the only handler among dock.py's six with no try/except around the manager call. Its five siblings all wrap. (DIAG-7)

Both errors.py handlers have no try/except at all, while every dock.py and maintenance.py write handler wraps in HomeAssistantError. errors.py also has no `_LOGGER.debug("... complete: %s", payload)` trace line, which every other handler in the two sibling modules has.

`await ...async_save()` is INSIDE the try in `_handle_set_maintenance_interval` (wrapped as HomeAssistantError) but OUTSIDE it in `_handle_set_dock_event_count` (services/dock.py:129) and `_handle_reset_maintenance` (services/maintenance.py:71), where a storage failure escapes raw. Same operation, three lines apart, two error contracts.

`set_maintenance_interval` is the only handler that bypasses the manager entirely and writes `manager.data[...]` inline. Every other write in these modules goes through a subsystem-manager method that owns the storage shape. It is consequently the only write with no validation layer available to it.

Manager-resolution has three forms in the package for one question: `get_manager(hass)` (bare `hass.data[DOMAIN][DATA_RUNTIME]`, raises KeyError) in dock.py/maintenance.py; `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_RUNTIME)` + None check in setup.py; `hass.data.get(DOMAIN, {}).get(DATA_ERROR_TRACKER)` + None check in errors.py. Only errors.py's produces a caller-readable reason.
`reset_maintenance` validates `component`; `set_maintenance_interval` does not. Same file, same field name, same storage sub-tree. (DIAG-2)

`ErrorTracker.acknowledge` guards `if vacuum_entity_id not in root: return False` before touching the record; `ErrorTracker.recent_errors` calls `_ensure_record` unguarded and creates one. Same class, adjacent methods, opposite policies on the same untrusted input. (DIAG-5)

Dock gating vocabulary IS adapter-driven (`_vocab_set` reads `dock_events.triggers`); dock event-type/counter vocabulary is hand-copied into the service schema and twice more into dock/manager.py. Two policies about the same adapter block, ten lines apart. (DIAG-8)

`_handle_acknowledge_error` normalises `scope` with `.strip().lower()` AFTER the schema's case-sensitive `vol.In(("active_run","last_device","both"))` has already run — so `scope: "Both"` is rejected by the schema and the normalisation is unreachable. Same dead-defence pattern in `_handle_get_recent_errors`, whose `max(0, min(int(limit_raw), 50))` and `except (TypeError, ValueError)` both sit behind `vol.Coerce(int)` + `vol.Range(min=1, max=50)`.
`set_dock_event_count` is the only response in these modules that does not echo `vacuum_entity_id`.

`_display_label` produces user-facing English (`"Already Washing"`, `"Not Docked"`) directly from reason codes, and every `message` string in `build_action_status` is a hardcoded English literal. These reach the user through the card. Not i18n-routed anywhere in this path.
gotchas: `cv.entity_id` validates the STRING FORM only. It does not check the entity exists, that it is a vacuum, that it belongs to this integration, or that it is a managed vacuum. Three services here will happily create a permanent durable storage branch keyed by `vacuum.someone_elses_robot`. Add the `manager.data.get("vacuums", {}).get(vacuum_entity_id)` check yourself — services/setup.py:290 is the in-repo precedent.

`hass.services.async_call(..., blocking=True)` does NOT raise when the target entity is missing, disabled, or unavailable. HA filters those out (`helpers/service.py:764`, `[e for e in entity_candidates if e.available]`) and calls `log_missing`, which logs a warning and returns. If your handler treats "the call returned" as "the device did it", you will return a success-shaped response for a no-op. This is DIAG-1 and it is live today.

Manager methods are `**kwargs` passthroughs (core/manager.py:981-1003) to keyword-only subsystem methods. A missing key in the splatted dict is a `TypeError`, not a validated error. If your schema makes a field optional and something else is supposed to fill it in, verify what happens when the filler returns None — `resolved_call_data` returns the dict UNCHANGED when it cannot resolve `map_id`, and its docstring's claim that "the manager method will raise its own clear error" is not true of any manager method in this package.

`vol.Schema({...})` defaults to PREVENT_EXTRA, which is what makes `**call.data` splatting safe. If you ever add `extra=vol.ALLOW_EXTRA` to a schema, every `**call.data` handler in that module becomes a TypeError waiting for an automation with a stray key.

`get_manager(hass)` uses a bare subscript and raises KeyError if the runtime is gone. Fine during normal operation (services are unregistered on unload) but do not assume it in any code that can run during teardown.

Do NOT bind `manager.data` sub-dicts at construction time unless you are certain you run after `async_initialize`. `self.data` is reassigned wholesale at core/manager.py:313 (`self.data = await self.storage.async_load()`). DockManager gets away with `self._data = manager.data` only because it is constructed at line 357, forty lines later.

Storage writes here are mutate-then-save with no rollback. If `async_save()` fails, the in-memory change stands and the next unrelated save from any subsystem persists it — while your handler has already told the user the save failed. Snapshot the old value and restore it in the except if the operation is destructive.

Two entity types write the SAME storage slot as these services: `EufyVacuumMaintenanceIntervalNumber` (number.py:230-240) shares `data["maintenance"][vacuum][component]["interval_hours"]` with `set_maintenance_interval`, and it enforces bounds the service does not. If you add a service that writes a slot an entity also owns, replicate the entity's clamp — the entity's min/max protects the UI path only.

Brand component/event vocabularies are NOT shared. `adapters/eufy/maintenance_components.py` and `adapters/roborock/maintenance_components.py` overlap in only `filter`, `sensor`, `side_brush`. Roborock declares no `dock_events` block at all, so every dock action resolves to `missing_action_entity` there. Never hardcode a component or event key in a service schema; derive it from the adapter config or accept that brand 3 will be rejected by your own schema.

Python slice trap already sitting in this code: `items[-limit:]` with `limit == 0` returns the ENTIRE list. `ErrorTracker.recent_errors` has it (core/error_tracker.py:322) and is protected only by a schema floor of 1 that the handler's own clamp (floor 0) contradicts.

A `reason` key is not reliably present on failure responses. `acknowledge_error` and `get_recent_errors` include it only on the tracker-missing path; `reset_maintenance` includes it on two of three failure paths; the third is escalated to an exception instead. Callers must handle raised-error AND falsy-flag AND missing-reason. If you add a service, always emit `reason`.

All 60 findings survive verification; none is a false positive. I re-derived the two package-wide claims myself rather than trusting them: an AST sweep of every hass.services.async_register call site (75 registrations, not 79) confirms room_profiles.py:203 get_room_profiles is the sole registration with no schema, and a yaml.safe_load diff against services.yaml confirms exactly 16 registered services have no descriptor. I also read HA's installed cv.ensure_list (returns [] for None — the A3-ROOMS-2 CRITICAL) and homeassistant/helpers/service.py:765-773 (filters on e.available then only log_missing — the A6-DIAG-1 HIGH) rather than accepting either from the report.

I adjusted 18 severities, all downward, on three principles the reports applied inconsistently. (1) A failure that raises a visible error is at most MEDIUM; HIGH in this ladder is reserved for a wrong result with NO error shown — this moved A3-ROOMS-4 and A2-JOB-6. (2) A silent refusal returned in a supports_response payload is MEDIUM; a silent refusal with no response channel at all is HIGH — this separates A2-JOB-1 (no supports_response, docs promise a response it cannot return: the single strongest finding here) from A5-RUNPROF-1/2. (3) Reachable only by deliberate misuse of an undocumented power-user service caps at HIGH, not CRITICAL — A4-SETUP-2/5, which have no card or services.yaml surface at all.

Two findings needed real scrutiny before I let them stand. A5-RUNPROF-3 (overwrite discards steps) is a deliberate, comment-justified design choice, and its "the response MASKS the loss" claim is wrong — the back-filled room_group accurately describes the new plan; what survives is only the undocumented, unsignalled loss, so I cut it to MEDIUM. A4-SETUP-13 is the weakest item in the set and I nearly refuted it: the schema comment it cites is TRUE, the resolver does existence-check, and nothing is claimed-but-missing — it stands only as a LOW usability nit.

Three dedup notes for synthesis, since the count is inflated. resolved_call_data's false docstring ("the manager method will raise its own clear error") is reported four separate times as A2-JOB-9, A3-ROOMS-11, A5-RUNPROF-7 and A6-DIAG-7 — one fix at _common.py:57-60. The services.yaml descriptor gap is A1-WIRE-3 and A4-SETUP-15 — one sweep. The phantom-bucket-from-unvalidated-entity-id pattern is A2-JOB-8, A5-RUNPROF-8 and A6-DIAG-5, which the reports rated LOW/LOW/MEDIUM for identical mechanics; I normalised DIAG-5 to LOW.

On the contract, the highest-value thing this run captured is that the package has no single answer for "how does a handler report a refusal". I counted five incompatible conventions in live code: raise ServiceValidationError on the verb flag (run_profiles.py:190 — the correct one); raise only when reason equals one literal string (run_profiles.py:114/133/152/171 — the source of RUNPROF-2 and RUNPROF-6); wrap everything in HomeAssistantError (rooms.py, dock.py); return a {"status": "error"} dict (setup.py, four of five handlers); and log-and-return-None (adapter_config.py). A sixth, drop the refusal entirely, is A2-JOB-1. Any doc for a 17th module should state the flag-based raise as the pattern and name the other five as deviations to be migrated, because every one of them produced a finding in this run. The second contract fact worth writing down: async_save() belongs INSIDE the try in every mutating handler — it currently sits after the except block in all seven job_control handlers and outside the try in dock.py:129 and maintenance.py:71, while maintenance.py:95 has it inside, and that inconsistency alone is A2-JOB-7 and A6-DIAG-9.

SCOPE: all 60 findings walked against source. 58 real, 2 rejected as latent-only (A1-WIRE-6, A6-DIAG-10 — accurate code readings with no reachable service call). Two mechanisms were EXECUTED against the installed HA rather than reasoned about: cv.ensure_list(None) -> [] (confirms ROOMS-2's total wipe) and voluptuous PREVENT_EXTRA rejecting `carpet` (confirms ROOMS-4). services.yaml was parsed with the yaml module and diffed against every registration site, confirming WIRE-3/SETUP-15 (16 undescribed services) and ROOMS-4 (three services whose services.yaml required fields the schema rejects).

SEVERITY: 21 corrected, all downward, 0 upward. The dominant pattern in the over-rating was counting a refusal that IS returned in a supports_response payload (added:False+reason, overwritten:False+reason, room_count:0) as a "silent success" — it is a missing raise, not an undetectable failure. Second pattern: rating an admin-only service that self-heals on the next reload (SETUP-2/3/5) at the same level as a persistent data loss.

TOP 4 CONFIRMED, ranked: (1) A3-ROOMS-2 / A4-SETUP-1 / A3-ROOMS-1 — one root defect at two services. `map_bucket["rooms"] = managed_rooms` (room_crud.py:261) is an unconditional wholesale REPLACE sourced only from the frozen data["discovery"] snapshot, with no empty-input guard — and the identical hazard IS guarded in the sibling reconcile_room (room_crud.py:145-154) with a comment naming the exact failure. Three independent triggers: `enabled_room_ids:` blank in YAML, a migrated pre-state-machine install with no discovery cache, and the card's `?? []` at src/bindings/setup.js:288. save_managed_rooms has no supports_response, so the caller gets nothing back. (2) A2-JOB-1 — start_selected_rooms drops eleven distinct refusal reasons into a DEBUG log and is the only start service without supports_response. (3) A4-SETUP-6 — reject_rooms deletes by bare room id across EVERY map, permanently, unconfirmed, in a codebase whose stated identity model is vacuum+map+room. (4) A2-JOB-2 — start_zone_clean is the only start path with zero preconditions and overrides a running tracked job.

CROSS-CUTTING ROOT CAUSES worth one fix each rather than N: (a) resolved_call_data's docstring (_common.py:57-60) asserts "the manager method will raise its own clear error" — no manager method does; the actual failure is a bare TypeError from the ** splat. That single false comment is the whole of JOB-9, SETUP-7, ROOMS-11, RUNPROF-7 and DIAG-7. (b) get_manager (_common.py:35) is a bare double subscript with no None path, while five modules independently use the tolerant .get() form. (c) cv.entity_id validates form only; six services setdefault durable storage keyed on whatever string arrives, and services/setup.py:290 + adapter_config.py:145 prove the package can check membership.

IMPLEMENTATION CONTRACT (for a 17th module):
- Module surface is exactly `register(hass) -> None` and `SERVICES: tuple[str, ...]`; add the module to _DOMAINS in services/__init__.py. Teardown is only `hass.services.async_remove` per name — there is NO other cleanup hook, which is why WIRE-5's timer leaks.
- Handlers are module-level `_handle_x(hass, call)`; register() defines thin closures over them. Resolve the vacuum with `get_manager(hass)` and `resolved_call_data(hass, call)` — the latter fills map_id from the adapter's entities.active_map and returns call.data UNCHANGED when it cannot, so either subscript defensively or make map_id vol.Required.
- Every registration passes `schema=` (get_room_profiles is the sole exception, and that is finding WIRE-4). Schemas default to PREVENT_EXTRA — keep services.yaml fields and schema keys in lockstep or the HA-rendered form is uncallable (ROOMS-4).
- Reads: supports_response=True, no persist. Mutations: mutate, then `await manager.async_save()`. Put the save INSIDE the try (dock.py and maintenance.py's reset put it outside; job_control puts it after the except — DIAG-9, JOB-7).
- Error convention as actually practised: `except Exception as err: raise HomeAssistantError(f"Failed to X: {err}") from err` for infrastructure faults; `ServiceValidationError` for a refusal the caller can fix. The manager layer signals refusals by RETURNING `{<verb>: False, "reason": ...}` — it does not raise — so a handler must inspect the verb flag. Gate on the FLAG (`if not payload.get("saved")`, run_profiles.py:190), never on a reason literal; the reason-literal form is what makes RUNPROF-2 and RUNPROF-6 fall through.
- Response-shape rule the package violates and should state: a failure must not share the success key set. setup.py has both conventions in one file ({"status":"error"} at :211/:241/:269/:288 vs the success-shaped :184).
- Validation belongs at the schema boundary, not downstream: `color` is validated strictly by _hex_color_or_none in the same schema where clean_mode/fan_speed/water_level/floor_type are bare cv.string, and every one of those four is a finding (ROOMS-6, ROOMS-9, SETUP-10).
